documentation.range:
Pangshura sylhetensis is known from foothill areas adjoining the Brahmaputra valley of Bangladesh and India (Iverson 1992, Das 1995, Choudhury et al. 2000, Praschag and Fachbach 2001). This species appears to have one of the narrowest distributions of any south Asian geomydid (Das et al. 2010). It is present in Bhutan (I. Das pers. comm. 2018); and also possibly present in Myanmar but this needs confirmation. This species is found at elevations below 200 m above sea level.

It only occurs at a few small localities (associated with forest patches), and adding the area of all of these habitat patches together suggests an area of occupancy of presumably less than 500 km2.
documentation.population: Generally considered rare, Pangshura sylhetensis was not seen for decades (Das 1991); where populations have been found it is locally rare to very rare (Choudhury et al. 1997, 2000; Rashid and Khan, 2000). Praschag and Fachbach (2001) noted populations had been decimated in recent decades, and high densities were only to be found in well-protected areas, where highly fragmented occurrences are scattered along hundreds of kilometres of streams. In Bangladesh the species is severely depleted and critically endangered (S.M.A. Rashid pers. comm. 2011). A single population survives in Bangladesh in an approximately 15 km stretch of a river in the South East. In northeast India P. sylhetensis appears to be more widespread in different habitats than traditionally understood and may have larger populations in more locations than historically known.
documentation.habitats: Pangshura sylhetensis is confined to relatively small, clear, fast-flowing streams and may seasonally use nearby waterbodies with less or no current (Choudhury et al. 1997, Pawar and Choudhury 2000, Praschag and Fachbach 2001, Das et al. 2010). Females utilise different parts of the waterbodies than males and juveniles (Praschag and Fachbach 2001). Juveniles, males and small females can be found in shallow sections of rivers without strong current, whereas adult females occur exclusively in deeper river channels and pools of rivers (Das et al 2010). This species basks exclusively on emergent rocks or logs, often in groups of up to a dozen individuals of both sexes (Das et al. 2010). The animals are primarily herbivorous but take some animal prey; captives accepted a variety of vegetable and animal food items (Choudhury et al. 1997, Praschag and Fachbach 2001). Females reach up to 18.5 cm carapace length, males no more than 9.7 cm. Maturity is reached at 14 cm (females) or a little over 7 cm (males). Females produce clutches of 6–12 eggs. (Praschag and Fachbach 2001, Das et al. 2010). Age of maturity may be about six years; suggesting approximately 18 years for a generation length; there is no data available for longevity.
documentation.threats: Widespread local subsistence consumption of Pangshura sylhetensis occurs, while erosion, siltation and other forms of habitat damage are an issue, and the species is in demand for the high-end pet trade (Das 1991, Choudhury et al. 2000, Praschag and Fachbach 2001, Das et al. 2010). Two live specimens, in separate shipments, were reported as seized from illegal trade during the period 2000–2015 (CITES CoP17 Doc73). The species’ distribution is apparently fragmented, occurring only localised within protected areas, and occupying a very small collective area of occupancy within a large extent of occurrence. Most seizures in Bangladesh came from India in 2015 (P. Praschag pers. comm. 2018). Adult females in China currently fetch as much as $10,000 per animal (P. Praschag pers. comm. 2018).
documentation.measures:
Pangshura sylhetensis is included in CITES Appendix II, allowing international commercial trade in the species provided such trade is not detrimental to the species, and subject to national trade legislation. Pangshura sylhetensis (as Kachuga sylhetensis) is protected under Schedule I of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 (amended), which includes endangered species that may only be hunted under exceptional circumstances, under licence from both federal and provincial authorities. Legal protection status in Bangladesh is unclear.

Pangshura sylhetensis has been recorded from Kaziranga National Park, Manas Tiger Reserve, Nameri Wildlife Sanctuary, and Dibru-Saikhowa Wildlife Sanctuary (Assam), Ngengpui Wildlife Sanctuary (Mizoram), and Pakhui, India (Hanfee 1999, Choudhury et al. 2000, Praschag and Fachbach 2001). In situ conservation action by collecting nests and artificially incubating the eggs has been reported from Assam (Baruah et al. 2010).

Further surveys are needed, and natural history studies are desirable. Safeguarding the populations and the ecological integrity of the protected areas of the northeast will be key to the species’ survival. Ex situ conservation methods are needed.
documentation.use_trade: Pangshura sylhetensis is utilised for local subsistence collection, and collection for the high-end pet trade are key uses of this species. Pangshura sylhetensis appears in the pet trade in Delhi, but is generally claimed to be captive-bred; however, the species is very difficult to breed in captivity so there is some uncertainty about these claims.
documentation.rationale: Pangshura sylhetensis is a small, cryptic species with specialised habitat requirements for clear flowing streams; available information is that the species is generally rare, has declined in overall area of occurrence due to exploitation and habitat loss, and viable populations are now restricted to scattered occurrences in suitable stream habitat within protected areas. Overall a substantial (80% over three generations) decline in recent decades appears to have occurred, and the species continues to be threatened by habitat degradation and targeted collection for the high-end global pet trade. It additionally only occurs at a few small localities (associated with forest patches), and adding the area of all of these habitat patches together suggests an area of occupancy of presumably less than 500 km2.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Traditionally placed in the genus Kachuga, it was assigned to the subgenus Pangshura by Moll (1987); Pangshura was elevated to genus level by Das (2001).
